words.shortDefinition: Quantitative measure used to track performance against a reliability goal.
words.simpleDefinition: A specific, quantitative measurement used to track performance against a reliability goal — such as error rate or average latency. SLIs provide the raw data used to determine if a service is meeting its defined SLO.
words.longDefinition: Service Level Indicators (SLIs) are the precise metrics used to measure the actual performance of a service against its defined objectives. Common SLIs include request latency, error rates, and system throughput. Unlike high-level metrics, SLIs are directly tied to user experience and are used to calculate whether a service is meeting its SLO targets over a specific measurement window, such as rolling 30-day periods.
words.connector: Think of SLI like a real thermometer — the SLO is the target room temperature, while the SLI is the actual number you read off the wall.
words.techContext: Our primary SLI for the search service is the latency of the 'search-results' API endpoint.
words.exampleSentence: The SLI showed a sudden spike in 500 errors, indicating that we were about to breach our service level objective.
words.etymology: Acronym for Service Level Indicator.

codeExample.code:
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{status="200"}[5m])) 
/ 
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

words.shortDefinition: Target reliability goals defined for specific service level indicators.
words.simpleDefinition: A formal reliability target — like 99.9% availability — that a team agrees to meet for a specific service. SLOs act as the bridge between business expectations and engineering reality, guiding development priorities.
words.longDefinition: Service Level Objectives (SLOs) are specific, measurable goals used to define the desired reliability of a service. They are derived from business requirements and user expectations, such as '99% of requests must complete in under 500ms'. By setting clear SLOs, engineering teams can objectively measure their performance and make data-driven decisions about when to prioritize feature development versus reliability improvements.
words.connector: Think of SLOs like a course grade target — you aim for an 'A' (99.9%), and falling below it triggers extra study (fixing reliability).
words.techContext: We defined an SLO of 99.9% availability for our payment service to ensure a consistent experience for our customers.
words.exampleSentence: If we fall below our SLO, the team stops working on new features and focuses entirely on reliability until we're back within the target.
words.etymology: Acronym for Service Level Objective.

codeExample.code:
service: checkout
slo:
  - name: availability
    target: 0.999
    window: 30d
    indicator:
      metric: http_requests_total

words.shortDefinition: Maximum allowed unreliability for a service during a specific time window.
words.simpleDefinition: The formal allowance for system unreliability derived from an SLO — representing the total downtime or error count a team can 'spend' during a cycle. It provides a data-driven way to balance innovation risk against stability.
words.longDefinition: An error budget represents the amount of unreliability a service can tolerate before it violates its Service Level Objective (SLO). Calculated as 1 minus the SLO target, it provides a quantitative framework for managing risk. If a team has a surplus budget, they can release features more aggressively; if the budget is exhausted, they must pivot to reliability work to ensure they don't breach their uptime commitments.
words.connector: Think of an error budget like vacation days — you get a fixed amount per year to spend on 'adventures' (risky updates), but you can't exceed it.
words.techContext: We still have 50% of our error budget left for this month, so we can go ahead with the risky infrastructure migration tonight.
words.exampleSentence: The major outage yesterday consumed our entire error budget for the quarter, so all new releases are currently on hold.
words.etymology: from 'error' + 'budget' (allocation of resources).

codeExample.code:
slo_target: 99.9%
current_availability: 99.95%
remaining_error_budget: 0.05% 
status: "Budget healthy, deployments allowed"

words.shortDefinition: Number of unique values within a specific metric dimension or label.
words.simpleDefinition: The number of unique values within a single dimension or label of a metric — such as the number of unique user IDs. High cardinality can rapidly overwhelm monitoring systems, leading to increased storage costs.
words.longDefinition: Cardinality in observability refers to the number of unique combinations of label-value pairs for a specific metric. High cardinality occurs when dimensions contain many unique values, such as user IDs or transaction hashes. This can lead to a 'cardinality explosion', exponentially increasing the number of time-series stored in databases like Prometheus. Managing cardinality is critical for maintaining system performance and controlling the costs of monitoring infrastructure.
words.connector: Think of cardinality like drawers in a filing cabinet — having 5 regions (low) is easy to manage; having 1M user IDs (high) collapses the floor.
words.techContext: We accidentally crashed our Prometheus server by adding a high-cardinality label (order_id) to our 'order_processed' metric.
words.exampleSentence: To avoid cardinality explosions, we only use low-cardinality labels like 'region' or 'environment' for our core metrics.
words.etymology: from Latin cardinalis ('principal, chief').

words.shortDefinition: Monitoring request paths as they flow across multiple microservices and networks.
words.simpleDefinition: The practice of monitoring requests as they flow through complex microservice architectures — spanning multiple servers and networks. It stitches together individual 'spans' using unique IDs to provide a holistic view of a single transaction's path.
words.longDefinition: Distributed tracing is essential for debugging modern microservices where a single user action may trigger dozen of internal service calls. By propagating a unique trace identifier through every request header, the system can reconstruct the entire execution path. This visibility helps engineers identify which specific service in a long chain is responsible for errors or high latency, significantly reducing mean time to resolution.
words.connector: Think of distributed tracing like tracking a relay race baton — you see which runner held it longest and exactly where it was dropped.
words.techContext: Implementing distributed tracing was the only way we could understand the complex interactions between our 50 different microservices.
words.exampleSentence: Distributed tracing allowed us to visualize the entire lifecycle of a request as it hopped across different servers and data centers.
words.etymology: from 'distributed' + 'tracing'.

codeExample.code:
# Example propagation header
curl -H "traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01" \
     http://api.internal/v1/orders

words.shortDefinition: Tools providing granular visibility into application code execution and performance.
words.simpleDefinition: Application Performance Monitoring — specialized tools that provide granular visibility into code-level execution, database queries, and external API dependencies. They help developers identify specific slow functions and performance bottlenecks in real-time.
words.longDefinition: Application Performance Monitoring (APM) involves tracking the performance and availability of software applications. APM tools instrument application code to provide deep insights into execution time, stack traces, and database interactions. By monitoring the application layer directly, these tools help developers pinpoint the exact line of code or SQL query causing performance degradation. Modern APM solutions often incorporate distributed tracing and profiling to provide a comprehensive view of complex request lifecycles.
words.connector: Think of APM like a high-tech stethoscope for your app — it lets you listen to the heartbeats of individual functions to find where the blockage is.
words.techContext: Our APM tool automatically detected a slow-running SQL query that was causing the entire dashboard to lag.
words.exampleSentence: We use an APM agent to see exactly which line of code is responsible for the performance bottleneck.
words.etymology: Acronym for Application Performance Monitoring.

words.shortDefinition: Open-source time-series database and monitoring system using a pull-based model.
words.simpleDefinition: Industry-standard open-source monitoring system that 'scrapes' metrics from application endpoints and stores them in a time-series database. It provides a powerful query language, PromQL, for analyzing data and managing complex alerting rules.
words.longDefinition: Prometheus is a specialized monitoring platform designed for cloud-native environments. It periodically 'scrapes' metrics from target services via HTTP, storing them in a local time-series database. Its powerful query language, PromQL, enables complex data analysis, such as calculating error rates over time or identifying resource saturation. Prometheus also includes an Alertmanager to handle notifications based on predefined threshold violations.
words.connector: Think of Prometheus like a census taker — it periodically visits every house (service) to collect specific statistics and records them in a master database.
words.techContext: Our Kubernetes nodes are configured to expose an '/metrics' endpoint that Prometheus scrapes every 15 seconds.
words.exampleSentence: I wrote a PromQL query to calculate the 99th percentile latency of our API over the last 24 hours.
words.etymology: Named after the Greek Titan who brought fire to humanity.

codeExample.code:
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) 
/ 
rate(http_requests_total[5m]) * 100

words.shortDefinition: Visualization platform for creating interactive dashboards from various data sources.
words.simpleDefinition: The standard open-source platform for visualizing time-series data through interactive, customizable dashboards. It connects to various data sources like Prometheus or Elasticsearch, turning raw metrics into beautiful, human-readable charts, graphs, and alerts.
words.longDefinition: Grafana is a leading open-source dashboarding tool that integrates with dozens of data sources, including Prometheus, InfluxDB, and Elasticsearch. It allows teams to create unified visualizations that combine logs, metrics, and traces into a single glass-pane view. Its flexible alerting system and support for dynamic variables make it indispensable for monitoring real-time system health and communicating operational status across technical teams.
words.connector: Think of Grafana like a specialized news television station — it takes data from all over the world and presents it in easy-to-read graphics.
words.techContext: We created a Grafana dashboard to give the whole team a real-time view of our production error rates and server health.
words.exampleSentence: I added a new panel to the Grafana dashboard to track the number of successful sign-ups per hour.
words.etymology: Invented name, possibly related to 'graph'.

words.shortDefinition: Methodical problem-solving process used for identifying the fundamental origin of faults.
words.simpleDefinition: Systematic process of digging past surface symptoms to identify the original, fundamental cause of an outage or failure. RCA aims to identify systemic weaknesses and implement fixes that prevent the same problem from recurring.
words.longDefinition: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) is a systematic investigation into the underlying reasons for a system failure or outage. Rather than just addressing immediate symptoms, RCA seeks to identify the 'root' problem—whether it be a software bug, a misconfiguration, or a flawed process. The goal is to implement permanent remediations that prevent the same incident from recurring. RCA often culminates in a post-mortem document that shares findings and action items with the broader organization.
words.connector: Think of RCA like solving a mystery — you don't just find the broken window; you find who threw the rock and why they were there.
words.techContext: The Root Cause Analysis revealed that the outage wasn't caused by the new code, but by a misconfigured load balancer timeout.
words.exampleSentence: After every production incident, the team performs an RCA and publishes a post-mortem document.
words.etymology: from 'root' (origin) + 'cause' + Greek analysis ('a breaking up').

codeExample.code:
RCA: Database Outage
Symptom: All 500 errors
Root Cause: Disk space 100% full on DB primary
Fix: Automated cleanup of archive logs and increased disk alert threshold

words.shortDefinition: Measurement of how close a system resource is to its maximum capacity.
words.simpleDefinition: Metric measuring how 'full' or utilized a specific system resource is — such as CPU at 90% or a database connection pool at 95%. High saturation often precedes a rapid degradation in system performance.
words.longDefinition: Saturation is one of the 'Four Golden Signals' and measures the degree to which a system's resources are being utilized. It specifically tracks the most constrained resources, such as CPU, memory, or I/O bandwidth. As saturation approaches 100%, systems typically experience exponential increases in latency and a sharp drop in throughput. Monitoring saturation allows engineers to proactively scale resources before the system becomes unresponsive or begins dropping requests.
words.connector: Think of saturation like a freeway — when it hits 100% capacity, traffic doesn't just go slow; it often grinds to a complete, gridlocked halt.
words.techContext: Our saturation metric for the database connection pool was at 95%, so we knew we needed to increase the pool size immediately.
words.exampleSentence: The service started dropping requests because the network interface reached 100% saturation.
words.etymology: from Latin saturatio ('fullness').

codeExample.code: node_load1 / count(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}) * 100

words.shortDefinition: The four foundational metrics — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — for monitoring any user-facing service.
words.simpleDefinition: Google's SRE Book defined four signals that together cover nearly all production health problems: latency (how long requests take), traffic (how many requests arrive), errors (how many fail), and saturation (how full the constrained resource is). If you can only instrument four things per service, instrument these.
words.longDefinition: The four golden signals come from Chapter 6 of Google's SRE book (Beyer et al., 2016), distilled from years of running global-scale production systems. Latency measures how long it takes to serve a request — split by success and error paths, tracked at p50, p95, and p99 to expose tail behavior. Traffic measures demand placed on the system: requests per second, messages per second, or queries per second. Errors captures the rate of requests that fail, whether explicitly (HTTP 5xx) or implicitly (HTTP 200 with a wrong response body). Saturation tracks how full the most constrained resource is — often not CPU but a connection pool, a thread pool, or a queue depth. Together these signals detect virtually all user-facing degradation and serve as the starting coordinates for any investigation.
words.connector: Think of the four golden signals like vital signs in a hospital — pulse, blood pressure, temperature, and oxygen saturation. Four numbers that collectively tell you whether the patient is stable or crashing.
words.techContext: I built a single-page Grafana dashboard showing all four golden signals for every critical microservice so on-call engineers have one place to start any incident triage.
words.exampleSentence: The golden signals dashboard showed normal error and latency numbers but traffic had dropped to zero — which revealed a routing misconfiguration rather than a service crash.
words.etymology: Coined in Google's Site Reliability Engineering book (2016), chapter 'Monitoring Distributed Systems'; 'golden' emphasizes their universal applicability and high diagnostic value.

codeExample.code:
# Latency (p99)
histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

# Traffic
rate(http_requests_total[5m])

# Errors
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total[5m])

# Saturation
max(node_load1 / count without(cpu)(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}))

words.shortDefinition: Runaway growth in unique time-series combinations caused by high-cardinality metric labels.
words.simpleDefinition: When a metric label with an unbounded value set — like user_id or request_id — is added to a Prometheus metric, the number of tracked time series multiplies by the number of unique label values. Millions of series overwhelm the metrics store's in-memory index, causing out-of-memory crashes, slow queries, and runaway infrastructure bills.
words.longDefinition: A cardinality explosion is the sudden or gradual proliferation of active time series in a metrics store, triggered when high-cardinality dimensions are used as metric labels. Prometheus stores one time series per unique label-value combination. If a metric carries three labels each with 100 values, it creates 1,000 series. Replace one label with user_id (1,000,000 unique users) and you have 100,000,000,000 potential series — an amount that causes Prometheus to OOM before the thought is completed. The most common triggers are user-scoped labels, raw URL paths containing IDs, trace IDs mistakenly added to metrics, and unbounded error message strings. Prevention requires instrumentation standards enforced at code review, and detection relies on Prometheus's TSDB cardinality APIs or managed-platform alerting on series count growth.
words.connector: Think of cardinality explosion like a library catalogue system where each new book gets its own card for every possible attribute — title, author, color, weight, page count, and reader ID. It starts manageable and quietly becomes infinite.
words.techContext: We triggered a cardinality explosion by labeling our HTTP duration histogram with the raw endpoint path — every UUID-based URL like /orders/uuid generated a unique series, and Prometheus ran out of memory within 20 minutes of the deploy.
words.exampleSentence: The cardinality explosion was traced to a single label change in the payment service that added customer_id to a high-traffic counter metric.
words.etymology: from Latin cardinalis ('principal') + Latin explosio ('a driving out, bursting'); the metaphor captures the sudden, destructive growth pattern.

codeExample.code:
# Detect high-cardinality metrics — check which metrics have the most series
topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))

# Safe: bounded label
http_requests_total{status_code="500", region="us-east-1"}

# Dangerous: unbounded label — never do this
# http_requests_total{user_id="usr_a3f9b21c"}  -- one series per user!

words.shortDefinition: Contractual commitment to customers specifying minimum service levels and consequences for breach.
words.simpleDefinition: A Service Level Agreement is a formal, often legally binding contract that specifies the minimum reliability a vendor promises customers — typically with financial penalties like service credits if the commitment is missed. It sits above the internal SLO: your SLO target should be stricter than your SLA so you have a buffer before breach.
words.longDefinition: A Service Level Agreement (SLA) codifies the reliability promise made to customers in commercial terms. Unlike the internal SLO — which engineers own and use as a development signal — an SLA is a negotiated contract with business and legal consequences. SLAs define the measurement metric (availability, latency, error rate), the target threshold (99.9%), the measurement window (calendar month), and the remediation for breach (service credits, refunds, contract termination rights). Best practice from the SRE Workbook: set internal SLOs at least one nine tighter than the SLA. If your SLA is 99.9%, target a 99.95% SLO internally so that a near-miss on the SLO does not automatically trigger SLA consequences. Not every service needs an SLA — reserve them for externally-facing services where customers have commercial expectations.
words.connector: Think of an SLA like a warranty card — it is the written guarantee you hand to the customer, while the SLO is the internal quality standard your factory holds itself to so the warranty is never triggered.
words.techContext: Our enterprise SLA promises 99.9% monthly availability with a 10% service credit for each hour of breach, so our internal SLO is set to 99.95% to maintain a buffer.
words.exampleSentence: The three-hour outage breached our SLA threshold for two customers, triggering automatic service credit issuance for the affected billing period.
words.etymology: Acronym for Service Level Agreement; 'agreement' distinguishes it from an objective (SLO) — it is a bilateral contract, not a unilateral target.

codeExample.code:
# SLA vs SLO layering example
sla:
  availability: 99.9%
  window: calendar_month
  remedy: 10% service credit per hour of breach

internal_slo:
  availability: 99.95%   # 0.05% tighter — the safety buffer
  window: rolling_28d
  owner: platform-sre-team

words.shortDefinition: The speed at which a service is consuming its error budget relative to a sustainable pace.
words.simpleDefinition: Burn rate is the ratio of your current error rate to the error rate that would exactly exhaust the error budget at window end. A burn rate of 1 means you are on pace to use the budget perfectly. A burn rate of 14 means the budget will be empty in a fraction of the time — page someone immediately.
words.longDefinition: Burn rate (introduced in the SRE Workbook's alerting chapter) solves the fundamental problem with raw error-rate alerting: a service slowly accumulating errors may look acceptable instantaneously but will exhaust the budget long before the window closes. The formula is burn_rate = error_rate / (1 - SLO). For a 99.9% SLO (0.1% error budget), an error rate of 0.1% yields burn rate 1.0 — sustainable. An error rate of 1.44% yields burn rate 14.4, exhausting the monthly budget in two hours. Burn rate translates an instantaneous measurement into a forward-looking budget projection, making it the correct signal for SLO-based alerting. Multi-window alerting fires only when a high burn rate is confirmed across both a short window (confirming it is happening now) and a long window (confirming it is sustained, not a spike).
words.connector: Think of burn rate like a car's fuel consumption readout — not just how much fuel is in the tank, but how fast you are burning through it and how many miles you have left before empty.
words.techContext: Our PagerDuty integration fires a critical page when the 1-hour burn rate exceeds 14.4 for the checkout service, giving us less than two hours before SLO breach.
words.exampleSentence: The burn rate spiked to 36 during the deploy, meaning the entire monthly error budget would have been exhausted in under 50 minutes if we had not rolled back immediately.
words.etymology: Borrowed from aerospace — a rocket's burn rate is how fast it consumes propellant; in SRE, the 'propellant' is error budget.

codeExample.code:
# Burn rate for a 99.9% SLO (error budget = 0.001)
(
  1 - (
    rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[1h])
    / rate(http_requests_total[1h])
  )
) / 0.001

# Alert if burn rate > 14.4 (budget exhausted in < 2 hours)

words.shortDefinition: Service-layer monitoring framework covering Rate, Errors, and Duration per request.
words.simpleDefinition: Tom Wilkie's practical shorthand for the minimum viable dashboard for any microservice: Rate (requests per second), Errors (how many are failing), and Duration (how long they take). Apply RED uniformly across every service in your architecture and anomalies jump out immediately.
words.longDefinition: The RED method was introduced by Tom Wilkie of Grafana Labs as a service-focused simplification of Google's four golden signals. Where the golden signals also cover infrastructure (saturation), RED focuses exclusively on the service layer — the behavior that requests observe. Rate answers 'is there traffic and how much?', Errors answers 'how often do requests fail?', and Duration measures the distribution of request processing time (preferred over 'latency' because it is unambiguous about what is being timed). RED's power is uniformity: the same three-metric template applies to every microservice without customization. In Prometheus, a single histogram metric (request_duration_seconds) gives you Duration; a counter on total requests gives Rate; a counter filtering on error status codes gives Errors. Deviation from baseline across any of the three signals triggers investigation.
words.connector: Think of RED like taking vital signs for a service — if its pulse (rate), bleeding (errors), or fever (duration) deviates from baseline, something needs attention.
words.techContext: We applied the RED method uniformly across our 40 microservices with a shared Grafana dashboard template, which meant on-call engineers could triage any service without learning a custom dashboard layout.
words.exampleSentence: The RED dashboard caught the slowdown instantly — Duration had jumped from 50ms to 800ms at p99 while Rate and Errors were normal, pointing to an internal processing bottleneck rather than a dependency failure.
words.etymology: Acronym coined by Tom Wilkie (Grafana Labs) around 2015; RED builds on the four golden signals framework from Google's SRE Book.

codeExample.code:
# Rate: requests per second
rate(http_requests_total[5m])

# Errors: fraction of requests failing
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])
  / rate(http_requests_total[5m])

# Duration: p99 latency
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

words.shortDefinition: Resource-level diagnostic framework covering Utilization, Saturation, and Errors for every infrastructure component.
words.simpleDefinition: Brendan Gregg's systematic checklist for diagnosing hardware and infrastructure bottlenecks: Utilization (how busy is the resource as a percentage?), Saturation (is work queuing up waiting for it?), Errors (is the resource producing error events?). Apply USE to every resource in your system — the one where all three numbers are elevated is your bottleneck.
words.longDefinition: The USE method was developed by Brendan Gregg (Netflix, Sun/Oracle) as a discipline for infrastructure performance analysis. Where RED asks 'is my service healthy?', USE asks 'why is my hardware struggling?' Utilization is the average fraction of time a resource is busy — a CPU at 90% utilization is heavily loaded but not necessarily problematic. Saturation is the leading indicator: the queue depth, wait time, or number of processes blocked on the resource. A connection pool can be at 80% utilization but zero saturation (requests enter immediately); if utilization reaches 100% and saturation begins, connection timeouts follow rapidly. Errors captures resource-level failures: ECC memory errors, disk read errors, TCP retransmissions — signals invisible to application-layer monitoring that often precede hardware failures. The USE method works because it is a complete checklist: apply USE to CPUs, memory, disks, network interfaces, and connection pools; any resource with low utilization, zero saturation, and no errors is not your bottleneck.
words.connector: Think of USE like checking every pipe in a plumbing system — for each pipe, ask: how full is it, is there a backup forming, and is it leaking? The pipe causing all three problems is where you start your fix.
words.techContext: Applying the USE method to our database servers revealed that disk I/O utilization was at 95% and saturation was non-zero even when CPU and memory looked fine — the bottleneck was disk throughput, not compute.
words.exampleSentence: The USE method pointed us directly at the network interface — utilization was near 100%, packets were queuing, and we saw TCP retransmission errors that the application layer had never alerted on.
words.etymology: Acronym coined by Brendan Gregg; described in his 2012 article 'The USE Method' at brendangregg.com. USE complements the service-focused RED method by handling the resource layer beneath services.

codeExample.code:
# Utilization: CPU busy fraction
1 - avg(rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m]))

# Saturation: run-queue length
node_load1

# Errors: network packet drops
rate(node_network_receive_drop_total[5m])

words.shortDefinition: The foundational taxonomy of observability signals: logs, metrics, and distributed traces.
words.simpleDefinition: The three pillars taxonomy — logs, metrics, and traces — comes from Peter Bourgon's 2017 post and describes the three fundamental signal types that together provide visibility into distributed systems. Logs capture discrete events, metrics aggregate numbers over time, and traces follow requests across service boundaries.
words.longDefinition: The three pillars of observability framework defines the signal categories that observability tooling has historically been organized around. Logs are timestamped records of discrete events — rich in context, expensive to query at volume, most useful for deep post-incident investigation. Metrics are numeric time-series measurements, pre-aggregated and cheap to store, optimized for alerting and trend analysis but structurally limited to low-cardinality dimensions. Traces capture the causal chain of a single request as it traverses multiple services — a tree of spans with start times, durations, and attributes. The three pillars are useful as an introduction but imperfect as an architecture goal: the three signal types overlap significantly, and siloing them in separate tools creates correlation gaps that incidents fall into. OpenTelemetry's unified data model, which derives logs, metrics, and traces from the same structured event stream, is the practical response to those gaps.
words.connector: Think of the three pillars like a crime scene investigation kit — fingerprints (logs), statistics on where crimes occur (metrics), and GPS tracking the suspect's route (traces). Each tells you something different; you need all three to understand the full picture.
words.techContext: We had all three pillars instrumented — logs in Loki, metrics in Prometheus, traces in Tempo — but they were separate silos with no correlation IDs, so during incidents we had to manually cross-reference timestamps across three UIs.
words.exampleSentence: After adopting OpenTelemetry, our three pillars became correlated: every log entry carries the trace ID of the request that generated it, so a single click navigates from a Grafana alert to the relevant trace.
words.etymology: Taxonomy introduced by Peter Bourgon in his 2017 blog post 'Metrics, Tracing, and Logging'; popularized by the CNCF observability landscape documentation.

words.shortDefinition: The desensitization of on-call engineers caused by excessive or low-signal alert volume.
words.simpleDefinition: Alert fatigue occurs when engineers receive so many pages — many of them low-signal or auto-resolving — that they stop treating alerts as urgent. The result is delayed responses to real incidents, missed pages, and burnout. It is a system failure, not a personal one.
words.longDefinition: Alert fatigue is the progressive erosion of on-call responsiveness caused by sustained exposure to high alert volume with low actionability. Google's SRE Book identifies it as one of the primary failure modes of monitoring systems: when every alert demands immediate action but few actually represent user harm, engineers learn through experience that most pages can be ignored. The rational response to hundreds of weekly low-signal alerts is to stop treating any individual alert as urgent — which means real incidents also get delayed responses. Causes of alert fatigue include cause-based alerting (CPU spikes, disk pressure), alerts that auto-resolve without requiring action, thresholds set too low, and duplicate alerts from multiple monitoring systems. The cure is ruthless alert review: every alert that cannot be answered with a specific, documented action within minutes should be demoted to a ticket, suppressed, or deleted. PagerDuty's 2023 survey found that teams with more than 15 pages per week reported over half as non-actionable.
words.connector: Think of alert fatigue like the boy who cried wolf — after enough false alarms, the shepherd stops reacting, and the real wolf arrives to an undefended flock.
words.techContext: After our alert fatigue audit, we reduced weekly pages from 80 to 12 by converting cause-based alerts to tickets and tightening thresholds on the remaining pages to require sustained SLO-impacting burn rates.
words.exampleSentence: Alert fatigue had gotten so bad that engineers were silencing PagerDuty by default, which is why the real database outage went unacknowledged for 40 minutes.
words.etymology: from 'alert' (Italian all'erta, 'on the watch') + Latin fatigatio ('weariness, exhaustion'); the compound describes the exhaustion specific to alarm overload.

words.shortDefinition: Alerting strategy that pages on observed user impact rather than on internal resource metrics.
words.simpleDefinition: Alerting on what users actually experience — elevated error rates, slow checkout flows, failed logins — rather than on infrastructure metrics like CPU or disk usage. Symptom-based alerts are actionable by definition: if the symptom exists, users are harmed and human intervention is justified.
words.longDefinition: Symptom-based alerting is the Google SRE Workbook's recommended alerting philosophy, contrasted with cause-based alerting. A symptom is an observable degradation in user experience: the SLO error budget is burning at a high rate, the checkout success rate has dropped below target, or the API's p99 latency has crossed a user-perceptible threshold. A cause is an internal resource condition — CPU at 90%, disk at 80%, queue depth growing — that may or may not have user impact. The SRE Workbook rule: page on symptoms, ticket on causes. Symptom alerts have near-zero false positive rate because they are grounded in actual user harm. Cause alerts have high false-positive rates because most internal resource anomalies self-resolve or have no user impact. Practical implementation: define SLOs per service, use burn-rate alerting as the primary paging mechanism, and relegate cause-based signals to dashboards and low-urgency ticket rules.
words.connector: Think of symptom-based alerting like an emergency room triage system — doctors don't page the surgeon every time a patient's temperature is slightly elevated; they page when the patient is actually deteriorating.
words.techContext: Switching from cause-based to symptom-based alerting cut our weekly page count by 70% because we stopped waking engineers for CPU spikes that never translated into user-visible degradation.
words.exampleSentence: Symptom-based alerting fired immediately when the payment gateway error rate hit 3%, while our old CPU alerts would have stayed silent because the servers were handling the load fine — just returning errors.
words.etymology: from Greek symptoma ('that which has befallen') + 'alerting'; the philosophy roots the alert in observed user harm rather than hypothesized internal cause.

words.shortDefinition: Scheduled assignment of engineers to primary pager responsibility for a defined time period.
words.simpleDefinition: The structured schedule that assigns specific engineers to be the first responder for production alerts during a defined shift — typically one week at a time. A healthy rotation has enough participants that no engineer is on call more than every four to six weeks, a clear secondary escalation path, and a documented handoff process.
words.longDefinition: An on-call rotation is the operational mechanism that ensures a human is reachable and responsible for production incidents at all times. Rotations are typically organized as primary (first to be paged) and secondary (escalation if primary does not acknowledge within a defined window, often 5 minutes). The rotation size — how many engineers share it — directly determines on-call burden per person. Google's SRE Book recommends rotations of at least 8 engineers to keep on-call frequency at roughly one week per two months per engineer. Smaller rotations cause burnout and reduce the pool of people deeply familiar with the systems. Best practices include explicit handoff documents between shifts (incidents in progress, known fragile areas, upcoming risky deployments), compensation policy for after-hours pages, and postmortem requirements to address noisy alerts. Follow-the-sun rotations, where different regional teams cover daytime hours in their time zone, eliminate overnight coverage for global services.
words.connector: Think of on-call rotation like a hospital residency schedule — specific people are assigned responsibility for specific shifts, there is always a clear escalation path, and nobody is on call indefinitely.
words.techContext: We moved from a 4-person to an 8-person on-call rotation after burnout data showed engineers were being paged an average of 5 nights per week during their on-call weeks.
words.exampleSentence: The on-call rotation handoff doc noted that the batch job was flaky on Monday mornings, which saved the incoming engineer 30 minutes of investigation when it fired at 2 AM.
words.etymology: from 'on call' (available for emergency duty) + 'rotation' (Latin rotatio, 'a turning'); reflects the cyclic assignment of duty among team members.

words.shortDefinition: Pre-agreed rules governing team behavior at different levels of error budget consumption.
words.simpleDefinition: A written agreement — negotiated before any crisis — that defines exactly what the team does when the error budget is healthy (ship freely), running low (slow down risky deploys), or exhausted (feature freeze, reliability sprint). Without a policy, 'error budget exhausted' is just a number on a dashboard.
words.longDefinition: An error budget policy is the governance document that gives the error budget mechanism teeth. Defined in the SRE Workbook as a critical artifact for making SRE work in practice, the policy specifies the team's response at each stage of budget consumption: above 50% remaining allows full velocity; 10-50% remaining triggers caution (risky deployments require extra review, reliability backlog work is started); below 10% triggers a feature freeze and reliability sprint; exhausted triggers a hard stop and leadership notification. The policy must also address override authority (who can approve a risky deployment when the budget is low), budget reset rules, and persistent-breach protocols (when three consecutive windows exhaust the budget, the SLO target itself is reconsidered). The policy is agreed between the SRE team, the development team, and product leadership when things are calm — not negotiated during an incident. A policy that is consistently overridden in practice is worse than no policy, because it destroys the credibility of the entire SLO mechanism.
words.connector: Think of an error budget policy like a household financial plan — you agree in advance what happens when your savings hit 50%, 10%, and zero, so those conversations don't happen in a panic when the account is already empty.
words.techContext: When our error budget hit 10% at mid-month, the policy automatically triggered an engineering sprint pivot: all new feature work paused, and three engineers were reassigned to addressing the flaky batch job causing the burn.
words.exampleSentence: The error budget policy was what turned 'the budget is running low' from an uncomfortable conversation into a pre-agreed engineering decision — no negotiation required.
words.etymology: from 'error budget' (SRE Workbook term) + 'policy' (Latin politia, 'civil administration'); the policy operationalizes the budget as a governance mechanism.

codeExample.code:
error_budget_policy:
  service: checkout-api
  slo: 99.9%
  window: 28d
  triggers:
    - threshold: 50%_remaining
      action: normal_velocity
    - threshold: 10%_remaining
      action: caution_mode  # risky deploys need extra review
    - threshold: 0%_remaining
      action: feature_freeze  # reliability sprint mandatory

words.shortDefinition: A Prometheus metric type that pre-computes quantile values client-side over a sliding time window.
words.simpleDefinition: A Prometheus metric type that calculates percentiles (p50, p95, p99) directly in the client application, rather than storing raw observations in a histogram. Summaries are accurate for a single instance but cannot be aggregated across replicas — making histograms the preferred choice in distributed systems.
words.longDefinition: In Prometheus's data model, a summary is one of four metric types alongside counters, gauges, and histograms. A summary instrument in the client library records observations (typically request durations) and calculates configured quantiles — such as the 50th, 95th, and 99th percentiles — over a configurable sliding time window. The calculated quantile values are then exposed directly as metric samples. The critical limitation: summary quantiles are computed per-process client-side. Two instances of the same service produce two independent quantile calculations, and Prometheus cannot meaningfully aggregate them into a fleet-wide percentile. For example, summing two p99 values does not produce the fleet p99. This limitation makes histograms — which store distribution buckets that can be aggregated in PromQL using histogram_quantile() — the preferred instrument for latency measurement in replicated services. Summaries remain useful for single-instance metrics or when the quantile calculation must be exact rather than approximate.
words.connector: Think of summary metrics like each chef in a restaurant calculating their own average plating time — the numbers are accurate per chef but you cannot average the averages to find the restaurant's true mean.
words.techContext: We replaced summary metrics with histograms across all our services when we moved to Kubernetes, because a summary's per-replica quantiles could not be aggregated to answer 'what is the p99 across all ten pods?'
words.exampleSentence: The summary metric was showing a healthy p99 of 120ms, but switching to histograms revealed the fleet-wide p99 was actually 850ms because a subset of replicas were misbehaving.
words.etymology: from Latin summarium ('a summary, an abridgment'); in Prometheus terminology, a 'summary' produces a pre-computed statistical summary of observations.

words.shortDefinition: The process of linking multiple alerts or anomalies across services to a single underlying root cause, reducing the noise a responder must triage during an incident.
words.simpleDefinition: When one root-cause failure triggers dozens of downstream alerts — a database restart fires alerts in six dependent services simultaneously — event correlation groups those related alerts together and identifies the probable root event. Without it, a responder faces 40 firing alerts for what is actually one problem. With it, they see one grouped incident with the probable origin highlighted.
words.longDefinition: Event correlation is the observability practice and tooling capability that groups related monitoring signals — alerts, anomalies, log patterns, trace errors — and associates them with a single causal event, reducing alert noise and accelerating root-cause identification during incidents. The need arises because distributed systems have cascading failure modes: one unhealthy database, one certificate expiry, or one misconfigured deployment can simultaneously trigger alerts in dozens of dependent services. Without correlation, the on-call engineer sees those downstream alerts in isolation and must manually trace upstream dependencies to find the origin — a process that can take tens of minutes during an incident. Event correlation approaches: topological correlation (using the service dependency graph to filter downstream noise — if service A depends on service B and B fires an alert first, A's alerts are correlated as downstream symptoms), temporal correlation (grouping alerts that fired within a short time window as likely related), and ML-based correlation (learning alert co-occurrence patterns from historical incident data). Practical implementations include Datadog Event Management, PagerDuty AIOps, and Grafana Incident. The prerequisite for effective correlation is a complete and accurate service dependency map, which makes service maps and distributed tracing critical companion capabilities. From an SLO perspective, event correlation reduces MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) and MTTR (Mean Time to Respond) by shortening the triage phase of incident response.
words.connector: Think of event correlation like a flight incident investigator — rather than treating each cockpit warning light as an independent failure, they recognize that three simultaneous alarms all trace back to a single hydraulics leak.
words.techContext: After enabling event correlation in our alerting platform, the 47-alert storm caused by a single Kafka broker restart was grouped into one incident card showing the Kafka broker as the probable root and all dependent consumer services as downstream symptoms.
words.exampleSentence: Event correlation cut the time from first alert to identified root cause by 22 minutes — instead of triaging 34 individual firing alerts, the on-call engineer opened one incident card showing the database failover as the common origin.

codeExample.code:
# PagerDuty Event Intelligence: alert grouping configuration
alert_grouping:
  type: intelligent          # ML-based temporal + topological correlation
  time_window: 5m            # group alerts firing within 5 minutes
  recommended: true          # auto-group based on past incident patterns

# Datadog Event Management: service topology correlation
# Alerts on services downstream of a failing dependency are
# automatically grouped as 'related alerts' in the incident timeline
# when the upstream service has an open alert.

words.etymology: From Latin 'eventus' (outcome, occurrence) + Latin 'correlatio' (mutual relationship, from co- + relatio). The compound entered observability and IT operations vocabulary from telecommunications fault management in the 1990s, where correlating network alarms to root faults was a foundational problem.

words.shortDefinition: Mean Time to Detect; the average elapsed time between when a failure begins affecting users and when the first alert fires, measuring how quickly the monitoring system notices a problem.
words.simpleDefinition: MTTD measures the gap between when something goes wrong and when your monitoring system tells someone about it. A 2-minute MTTD means failures are detected almost immediately; a 25-minute MTTD means users have been experiencing the problem for 25 minutes before anyone is even paged. MTTD is the first link in the incident response chain — every subsequent phase (diagnose, fix, restore) starts the clock from when the detect phase ends.
words.longDefinition: Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) is the average elapsed time from the moment a failure begins causing user-visible impact to the moment the first human or automated system is notified. It is the first phase in the MTTR breakdown: MTTD + MTTDI (Mean Time to Diagnose) + MTTF (Mean Time to Fix) = MTTR (Mean Time to Recover). MTTD is directly influenced by monitoring design choices. Factors that shorten MTTD: symptom-based alerting with burn-rate thresholds close to the SLO (rather than lagging indicators), short evaluation windows in alerting rules (5-minute windows detect sooner than 1-hour windows, at the cost of more false positives), synthetic monitoring that probes from outside the service (detects user-visible failures that internal metrics miss), and alert delivery reliability (a page that takes 10 minutes to route adds 10 minutes to MTTD). Factors that lengthen MTTD: cause-based alerting that requires internal metrics to saturate before firing, long alert evaluation windows, missing instrumentation for new features, and alert fatigue that causes pages to be muted. For SLO-critical services, MTTD is often tracked as a secondary operational metric alongside error budget consumption. A high MTTD means failures consume error budget for longer before detection begins.
words.connector: Think of MTTD like the smoke detector sensitivity setting — a sensitive detector triggers within seconds of a small fire (short MTTD), while a desensitized detector only triggers when the room is already full of smoke (long MTTD).
words.techContext: After implementing multi-window burn-rate alerting, our payment service MTTD dropped from 18 minutes to 4 minutes because the new rules fired on fast error budget consumption rather than waiting for aggregate error rates to cross a static threshold.
words.exampleSentence: The post-incident review showed MTTD was 31 minutes because the service had no synthetic probe monitoring and the internal metrics alert required a sustained 15-minute breach before firing.

codeExample.code:
# Measure MTTD indirectly: time from incident start to first alert
# Track alert evaluation lag using Prometheus's own metrics
rate(prometheus_rule_evaluation_duration_seconds_sum[5m])
/ rate(prometheus_rule_evaluation_duration_seconds_count[5m])

# Alert evaluation interval matters for MTTD:
# evaluation_interval: 15s  → can detect within 15s of condition onset
# evaluation_interval: 1m   → detection delayed by up to 1m

# In Grafana: track time-to-first-annotation per incident
# as a custom metric submitted by your incident tool webhook

words.etymology: Acronym for Mean Time to Detect. Part of the MTTR (Mean Time to Recovery) family of operational metrics. 'Mean' indicates an average across multiple incidents; 'detect' specifically refers to the observation phase, distinguishing it from the response and repair phases.

words.shortDefinition: The ability of a system to continue serving partial or reduced functionality when a dependency fails.
words.simpleDefinition: Designing services so that when a non-critical dependency is unavailable, the system returns reduced-but-useful results rather than failing completely. Graceful degradation is the difference between 'checkout works but shows no recommendations' and 'checkout is completely down.'
words.longDefinition: Graceful degradation is the architectural discipline of designing system responses to dependency failures along a spectrum rather than as a binary success/failure. When a non-critical service is unavailable, the system substitutes a fallback: cached data, a simplified response, a default value, or a polite message. The critical design question is which dependencies are on the critical path (their failure must fail the request) versus which are non-critical (their failure should degrade the response but not block the user). Amazon's SRE practices popularized the explicit notion of 'feature dependencies vs critical-path dependencies': recommendations and review counts are feature dependencies; inventory availability is a critical-path dependency. Graceful degradation requires designing fallback behaviors at development time, not under production pressure, and testing those fallbacks regularly (chaos engineering is the formal practice for this). From the SLI perspective, graceful degradation allows you to define a 'quality SLI' that separately tracks full-featured versus degraded-but-functional responses.
words.connector: Think of graceful degradation like a restaurant that can still serve dinner when the dessert chef calls in sick — customers get the main course without apology, rather than the restaurant closing entirely.
words.techContext: We implemented graceful degradation in our product page by falling back to a static 'New arrivals' list when the personalization service was unavailable, keeping the page functional for all users during the outage.
words.exampleSentence: Graceful degradation saved the launch — when the recommendation engine timed out under traffic load, the homepage showed curated static content instead of a 500 error, and conversion rates dropped only 3% instead of to zero.
words.etymology: from Latin gratia ('favor, elegance') + degradare ('to reduce in rank'); 'graceful' implies the reduction happens elegantly, preserving user experience as much as possible.

words.shortDefinition: A numeric metric derived by counting or aggregating log entries that match a defined filter, turning high-cardinality log data into low-cardinality time-series for alerting and dashboarding.
words.simpleDefinition: A log-based metric extracts a number from your logs by counting matching entries — for example, counting every log line containing 'payment_failed' to produce a time-series of payment failure events per minute. It lets you create alerts and charts from log data without changing any application code or adding new instrumentation.
words.longDefinition: Log-based metrics bridge the gap between the high-fidelity context of logs and the efficient queryability of time-series metrics. The mechanism: a log aggregation platform (Datadog, Grafana Loki, Google Cloud Logging, AWS CloudWatch Logs Insights) watches the incoming log stream and applies a filter expression — matching on a log field, a regex pattern, or a structured attribute. Each matching log entry increments a counter or contributes to an aggregate (count, sum, average of a numeric field). The result is a metric time-series with configurable labels derived from log fields. Use cases: counting specific error messages or exception types that are not already exposed as metrics by the application, deriving business event metrics (order_placed, user_signup) from application logs without modifying service code, tracking log-level distribution (how many WARNs vs ERRORs per minute), and extracting durations from log messages to build latency histograms without full distributed tracing deployment. Trade-offs: log-based metrics add latency compared to directly instrumented metrics (they depend on log ingestion pipeline latency, typically 10–60 seconds), and they inherit log sampling — if logs are sampled at 10%, the derived metric will undercount by 90%. For critical SLO measurements, directly instrumented metrics are preferred. Log-based metrics are most valuable for one-off investigations, legacy services without metrics instrumentation, and low-volume event counting where sampling is not applied.
words.connector: Think of log-based metrics like a bank teller manually tallying transaction slips to count how many transfers exceeded $10,000 today — you extract a count from an unstructured record stream without requiring changes to the underlying system.
words.techContext: We added a log-based metric to count 'payment_gateway_timeout' log lines from the legacy billing service, which had no Prometheus instrumentation. The metric fed an alert that caught a timeout spike three weeks before the service was due for re-instrumentation.
words.exampleSentence: A log-based metric on the 'NullPointerException' pattern gave us an alert before the bug was formally reported — the error had been appearing in logs at low frequency for two days before any user complained.

codeExample.code:
# Datadog Log-Based Metric definition
name: payment.failures.count
type: count
filter:
  query: "service:payment-service status:error @error.type:PaymentDeclined"
group_by:
  - facet: "@http.status_code"
    path: "@http.status_code"
    type: facet

# Grafana Loki: log-based metric via LogQL
# Count error log lines per service per minute
sum by (service) (
  count_over_time(
    {job="production"} |= "ERROR" [1m]
  )
)

words.etymology: Compound of 'log' (chronological record of events) + 'based' (derived from) + 'metric' (Greek metron, a measure). The concept emerged as log aggregation platforms added server-side processing pipelines, enabling the transformation of unstructured event streams into structured time-series data — a capability popularized by Splunk in the late 2000s and later adopted by Datadog, Loki, and CloudWatch.

words.shortDefinition: A single structured record emitted per unit of work containing every field that might be useful for future investigation.
words.simpleDefinition: A wide event is one rich JSON record per request — containing user ID, endpoint, latency, status code, feature flags, region, deployment version, and dozens of other fields simultaneously. Because all fields travel together, you can answer any combination of 'who, where, when, what' questions at query time without ever adding new instrumentation.
words.longDefinition: Wide events are Honeycomb's answer to the fundamental limitation of pre-aggregated metrics: the most useful debugging fields — user_id, request_id, session_id, feature_flag_variant — are exactly the high-cardinality fields that traditional metrics cannot store. A wide event inverts the instrumentation philosophy: instead of emitting many narrow metrics, each answering a specific pre-formulated question, emit one wide structured record per request containing every field you might conceivably want. The key insight is that when all fields travel together in a single event, you can slice by any combination of dimensions at query time — no new deploy, no new metric, no new log statement. OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions define a standardized vocabulary for wide-event fields (http.request.method, user.id, server.address, etc.) so events are queryable with consistent field names across all services. Wide events are the atomic unit of the 'observability' paradigm as described in Majors and Fong-Jones's 'Observability Engineering', distinguishing it from traditional monitoring.
words.connector: Think of a wide event like a detailed receipt from a restaurant — rather than a single total, it itemizes every dish, the server, the table number, the time, and the loyalty account. Any future question about that visit can be answered from a single document.
words.techContext: After switching to wide events, we traced a subtle checkout bug to a specific combination of subscription_plan='enterprise' AND feature_flag='new_tax_engine'=true AND region='eu-west-1' — a correlation impossible to discover from our old narrow metrics.
words.exampleSentence: Wide events meant the on-call engineer could answer 'is this slowness affecting only free-tier users in Asia?' in one Honeycomb query rather than correlating three separate dashboards.
words.etymology: Coined by Charity Majors and the Honeycomb team; 'wide' describes the number of fields in each event record — contrasted with 'narrow' events (individual metrics with few dimensions).

words.shortDefinition: Manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales with service growth and produces no enduring system improvement.
words.simpleDefinition: Google's SRE Book defines toil as work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, and grows proportionally with service load — the antithesis of engineering work. The SRE principle is that toil should never exceed 50% of an engineer's time; time above that cap must be invested in eliminating the toil's root cause.
words.longDefinition: Toil is a formally defined concept in the SRE discipline, distinct from overhead or ordinary work. The SRE Book specifies six properties of toil: it is manual (a human executes it, even if running a script); repetitive (done more than once, and will be done again); automatable (a machine could do it if someone built the automation); tactical (reactive and interrupt-driven rather than strategic); no enduring value (the service is back to the same state it was in before the work); and scales with service growth (as traffic doubles, the toil doubles). The canonical example is a weekly manual cert rotation, a one-click-but-required approval for every deployment, or manually restarting a service that crashes on the 15th of every month. Google's SRE Book mandates that no SRE team should spend more than 50% of their time on toil. Time beyond that cap must be invested in engineering work that eliminates the toil permanently — automation, better monitoring, architectural fixes. The 50% cap is both a cultural principle and a measurable operational target.
words.connector: Think of toil like bailing water from a leaking boat by hand — it keeps the boat afloat but does nothing to fix the hull. Engineering work patches the hull so you never have to bail again.
words.techContext: Our toil audit revealed that manual certificate renewals, on-call runbook steps, and deployment approval forms consumed 65% of the SRE team's time — well above the 50% cap, which justified a quarter-long automation sprint.
words.exampleSentence: Automating the weekly database compaction runbook eliminated 4 hours of toil per week per SRE, freeing them for the reliability improvements that reduced our incident rate by 40%.
words.etymology: from Anglo-French toiler ('to pull apart, struggle'); in SRE, coined as a precise technical term by the Google SRE team to describe unrewarding operational work in the landmark 'Site Reliability Engineering' book (2016).

words.shortDefinition: The process of forecasting future resource requirements and provisioning headroom before traffic growth causes saturation.
words.simpleDefinition: Capacity planning is the practice of projecting future load based on historical growth trends and provisioning enough compute, memory, storage, and network headroom so that saturation does not occur before scaling can be triggered. It converts reactive firefighting into proactive engineering.
words.longDefinition: Capacity planning in SRE is a continuous, quantitative practice that answers: 'given our current growth rate, when will we saturate each resource, and what must we provision to maintain our SLOs through that growth?' The SRE Book dedicates a full chapter to capacity planning as a core SRE responsibility. The process involves measuring current utilization per resource (CPU, memory, storage, network, database connections, external API rate limits), fitting growth models to historical usage trends, computing when each resource will cross its SLO-threatening saturation threshold, and provisioning before that threshold is reached — not after. Headroom — the margin between current utilization and saturation — is the key design target. A resource at 70% utilization with a 10x weekly growth rate has days of headroom; the same resource with linear 2% monthly growth has months. Capacity planning interacts with the USE method: USE identifies current saturation; capacity planning projects future saturation. Modern cloud environments make on-demand scaling easier but do not eliminate capacity planning — quotas, lead times for specialized instances, and budget constraints still require forward planning.
words.connector: Think of capacity planning like a logistics manager stocking a warehouse before a seasonal peak — they order inventory based on last year's sales data and growth trends, not by waiting until shelves are empty.
words.techContext: Capacity planning projected that our PostgreSQL disk would saturate in 8 weeks at the current write rate, giving us time to implement log partitioning and storage tiering before any SLO impact.
words.exampleSentence: Without capacity planning, we discovered our Redis memory limit when the eviction rate spiked at 3 AM — with it, we would have provisioned larger instances two weeks earlier.
words.etymology: from Latin capacitas ('spaciousness, power') + 'planning'; in SRE, formalized as a core discipline in Google's SRE Book (2016), Chapter 17.

words.pronunciation: MUL-tee WIN-doh MUL-tee BURN RAYT uh-LURT
words.shortDefinition: SLO alerting strategy using two time windows and two burn-rate thresholds to catch incidents and slow degradation while minimizing false pages.
words.simpleDefinition: The SRE Workbook's recommended alerting recipe: only page when a high burn rate is confirmed in both a short window (proving it is happening right now) and a long window (proving it is sustained, not a transient spike). Four tiers — two pages and two tickets — cover everything from 'budget gone in hours' to 'budget gone in days'.
words.longDefinition: Single-window burn-rate alerting has a fundamental flaw: a short window (1 hour) is sensitive to brief spikes that recover quickly and generate false pages; a long window (24 hours) is slow to detect fast-moving incidents. The SRE Workbook's multi-window multi-burn-rate recipe solves both problems by requiring a high burn rate to be confirmed in two windows simultaneously. The canonical recipe for a 99.9% SLO over 30 days: Page (critical) when burn rate > 14.4 confirmed in both 1h and 5m windows — budget exhausted in under 2 hours, action required immediately. Page (high) when burn rate > 6 confirmed in both 6h and 30m windows — budget exhausted in about 5 days, action within the hour. Ticket (warning) when burn rate > 3 confirmed in both 24h and 2h windows — budget exhausted in about 10 days, address by next business day. Ticket (low) when burn rate > 1 over a 3-day window — consuming budget faster than it replenishes, investigate this week. The dual-window confirmation dramatically reduces false pages: a 5-minute spike raises the short-window burn rate without affecting the long window, so no page fires.
words.connector: Think of multi-window alerting like a two-out-of-two key system on a nuclear launch — both the short-window key and the long-window key must confirm the problem before the alarm goes off. One bad reading alone is never enough.
words.techContext: After implementing multi-window burn-rate alerting for our checkout service, false-positive pages dropped from 30 per week to 2, while real incidents are still caught within 10 minutes of onset.
words.exampleSentence: The multi-window alert fired only when the burst of 5xx errors persisted beyond the 5-minute short window, confirming it was a real incident rather than a transient spike from a rolling restart.
words.etymology: Coined in Google's SRE Workbook (2018), Chapter 5 ('Alerting on SLOs'); 'multi-window' refers to using several time ranges simultaneously to confirm signal validity.

codeExample.code:
# Prometheus alerting rule: multi-window multi-burn-rate (99.9% SLO)
groups:
- name: slo-checkout
  rules:
  - alert: CheckoutBudgetCritical
    expr: |
      (1 - rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",code!~"5.."}[1h])
           / rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[1h])) / 0.001 > 14.4
      AND
      (1 - rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",code!~"5.."}[5m])
           / rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m])) / 0.001 > 14.4
    labels:
      severity: page
    annotations:
      summary: "Checkout SLO burning at >14.4x — budget exhausted in <2h"
